verdict.reasoning: Patient reports lip swelling after eating prawn soup: “I ordered a prawn soup… my lips start feeling a little weird… there is like a swelling on my upper lip.”
Timing is given as about 30 minutes: swelling developed “must have been like… I don’t know, half an hour maybe” after eating around 7 pm.
Patient states the swelling is increasing: “there is like a swelling on my upper lip and it’s kind of getting bigger… it feels like it’s getting worse.”
Patient reports difficulty breathing: in response to throat swelling question, “Yeah, actually I feel like I can’t breathe that well right now.”

Doctor asks about chest tightness and patient indicates possible involvement: “Do you feel like your chest is tight?” Patient: “I don’t know. Chest just generally feels a little difficult… it might be. I’m not sure.”
Patient has asthma: “Well, I generally have asthma… I do take [salbutamol] regularly, but I’ve always taken it. I generally have asthma.”

History of peanut allergy and prior severe reaction needing hospital: “So I have a peanut allergy as well… Has your mom ever said that you had to go to hospital because you had a severe allergic reaction? Patient: ‘Yeah, well, I was like six or something…’” indicating prior hospitalization.
Uses salbutamol inhaler: “I tell. I take. What’s it called? Salbutamol inhalus… Yeah. So I do take that regularly.”
Uses antihistamines but is unsure which: Doctor asks about antihistamines; patient: “Sometimes, but I don’t know which ones… I think I do get antihistamines for that, but I’m not sure which ones.”

The transcript does not address alcohol intake at the time of the current (prawn) reaction; alcohol is only mentioned for a past incident: “I remember that I was quite drunk, to be honest” (past episode). No statement about alcohol for the latest reaction.

No physical examination findings are described in the transcript; the consultation is history-based with no documented objective exam, so stating that none were recorded is consistent with the transcript’s content.
Doctor explicitly suspects anaphylaxis: “it sounds like you could be going into what we say, anaphylactic reaction.”

Acute lip swelling occurred after prawn ingestion: “I ordered a prawn soup… then my… lips start feeling a little weird… there is like a swelling on my upper lip.” Time course is acute (within ~30 minutes).

Respiratory symptoms with suspected anaphylaxis: patient says “I feel like I can’t breathe that well right now” and “Chest just generally feels a little difficult,” and doctor links this to an anaphylactic reaction in the assessment.

Doctor plans immediate emergency call: “I think we need to call an ambulance… hang on the line while I’ll call the ambulance… Mom, if you can call the 999… there is a suspected anaphylactic reaction and they need to come straight away.”
Doctor advises taking antihistamines if available: “Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around… So straight away, take the antihistamines in the meantime.”
Doctor advises not being alone until ambulance arrives: initially asks if anyone is with her, then: “Make sure that person’s with you till the ambulance comes.”

Doctor plans follow-up to address injections (EpiPen-equivalent): “Come out from the hospital. Do give us a ring back. We might need to sort you out with your injections and things like that.” This implies follow-up to assess need for self-injectable adrenaline.
